content: Shoulder dystocia is a specific type of childbirth complication in which the anterior shoulder of the baby becomes lodged behind the maternal pubic symphysis, making it difficult or impossible for the shoulder to pass through without significant intervention. This condition is diagnosed when the baby’s shoulders fail to deliver shortly after the head has emerged during vaginal delivery. To resolve shoulder dystocia, various obstetrical maneuvers are employed. Another technique, Jacquemier's maneuver (also referred to as Barnum's maneuver), involves delivering the posterior shoulder first to relieve the obstruction. In more severe cases, more invasive interventions may be necessary. These include Zavanelli's maneuver, which involves repositioning the baby’s head back into the uterus for delivery via Cesarean section, or intentionally fracturing the baby’s clavicle to reduce shoulder width. Although the exact definition of shoulder dystocia can be somewhat imprecise, it is estimated to occur in approximately 1% of vaginal deliveries. Certain risk factors are well-recognized, including maternal diabetes, fetal macrosomia (excessive fetal size), and maternal obesity. However, predicting its occurrence remains challenging. Even with appropriate obstetric management, shoulder dystocia can result in serious complications, such as brachial plexus injury to the baby, or in rare cases, fetal death, making it a critical obstetric emergency.
